mappings.note: The answer is an angle at the CIRCUMFERENCE standing on chord AB, reached from the central angle. Perpendicularity only supplies the central angle, and the equal tangent lengths are never used, so this is LO-4's tangents-chords-and-angles case.

Radius, tangent and the distance to the centre form a RIGHT triangle, and Pythagoras gives the radius. The right angle at the point of contact is the whole content, so LO-2. Only one tangent is drawn, so LO-3 cannot apply.
The 90 degrees at the point of contact plus the isosceles condition fixes the remaining angles. Perpendicularity is the load-bearing fact; no second tangent exists.
A CHORD subtending a right angle at the centre - pure chord geometry with no tangent anywhere in the configuration, which is the chord half of LO-4.
The intersecting-chords relation AE x EB = CE x ED, which is established by SIMILAR TRIANGLES - exactly what C-5.1-LO-4 names. No tangent theorem is involved, so C-5.2's outcomes do not fit.
The given datum is the angle a TANGENT makes with a CHORD, and the central angle is deduced from it. That tangent-chord angle is precisely LO-4; LO-2 supplies only the intermediate 90 degrees.
Solved entirely by equating tangent segments from A, B and C so that AP is half the perimeter of ABC. Equal tangents from an external point, so LO-3; no angle or right triangle enters.
A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle - its sides are CHORDS, each equal to the radius. Chord geometry, with no tangent in the figure at all.
Pythagoras on the right triangle formed by radius and tangent gives OP, and PR follows by adding a radius. The right angle at the contact point is the key step; only one tangent is present.
Two intersecting circles and their COMMON CHORD, bisected at right angles by the line of centres. Chord geometry; no tangent and no similarity argument.
The two 90 degree angles at the points of contact turn OPTQ into a quadrilateral whose remaining angles are supplementary. The equal LENGTHS of the tangents are never used, so LO-2 and not LO-3.
D is an external point to both circles, so DA = DC and DB = DC give AB = 2CD. Purely the equal-tangent-lengths property.

The 90 degrees between OC and the tangent PT is subtracted from the given 118 degrees, then an isosceles triangle on two radii finishes it. Perpendicularity is the engine; no second tangent and no inscribed-angle theorem.

Concentric circles: the chord of the outer circle TOUCHES the inner one, so the inner radius is perpendicular to it and bisects it. The perpendicularity at the point of contact is what makes the Pythagoras step legal.
Circumscribed quadrilateral, so AB + CD = BC + AD - a result that follows by pairing equal tangent segments at each vertex. LO-3, not LO-2: no right angle is used.
Same concentric configuration with numbers: the inner radius meets the chord at right angles and bisects it. Perpendicularity at the point of contact.

The 90 degrees at A plus a straight line at the centre fixes the third angle of triangle AOP. Only one tangent is drawn. Stem is garbled: it asks for the 'perimeter' of an angle where it means the measure.
The perimeter of triangle PCD collapses to PA + PB because each of C and D contributes a pair of equal tangent segments. Entirely the equal-tangent property.

Both theorems are indispensable: the RHS congruence rests on the right angles at the contacts (LO-2) and on OB = OC with the two equal tangents (LO-3), and only then does OA bisect the 120 degrees to give OA = 2AB.

Circles touching internally and externally, solved by adding and subtracting radii along the lines of centres. A tangency-configuration problem; no tangent line is drawn and no chord angle is used, so LO-4 is the closest of the three.
Concentric circles again: the common-centre radius is perpendicular to the touching chord, which licenses the Pythagoras step and the doubling.
Opposite sides of a circumscribed quadrilateral subtend supplementary angles at the centre - a consequence of the congruent pairs of tangent triangles at each vertex. LO-3 rather than LO-2.
The right angle at the point of contact makes OAT a right triangle, and the 30 degrees then gives AT by trigonometry. One tangent only.

The assertion is that tangents at the ends of a DIAMETER are parallel, which holds because each is perpendicular to that diameter - LO-2 directly. The reason offered (longest chord) is true but unrelated, which is what the item tests.
Assertion-reason on the tangent-radius right triangle: Pythagoras is legal only because the radius meets the tangent at 90 degrees, which is what the reason supplies.
